title: Factor Industry Resembles the Market | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional aggregates the Morningstar strategic beta category (560+ funds, ~$3 trillion) and finds the average dollar in factor-based products looks close to the market: slightly smaller and growthier than the Russell 3000 with very similar profitability. That implies factor crowding is not yet visibly compressing size and value premiums.

insights.claim: A rise in factor-based investing could mechanically lower expected size and value premiums, because more factor money bidding for small cap and value stocks raises their prices and lowers their expected returns.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: This is the core bear case on factor strategies; monitor aggregate factor-fund characteristics rather than assuming premiums persist unchanged.
insights.quote: If factor-based investors increase the overall demand for small cap and value stocks, the expected premium for these stocks could become lower.

insights.claim: The heterogeneity of factor products is the main reason factor growth need not compress premiums: different factor portfolios target different slices of the market, so their tilts can offset and leave a negligible net effect on expected returns.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Judge crowding risk on the net aggregate tilt of factor assets, not on headline growth of factor AUM.
insights.quote: However, there are many different types of factor-based portfolios that may result in targeting different areas of the market and exerting negligible net effect on expected return premiums.
insights.locator: However, there are many different types

insights.claim: The Morningstar strategic beta category spans more than 560 funds managing collectively about $3 trillion, all tracking indices that deliberately deviate from the market to raise return or manage risk.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Sizes the pool of money that could theoretically crowd factor premiums, giving a concrete denominator for crowding debates.
insights.quote: This category includes more than 560 funds, managing collectively about $3 trillion and tracking indices that deviate from the market based on specific objectives, such as increasing return or managing risk.
insights.locator: Plotting characteristics for the Morningstar strategic beta

insights.claim: Aggregated as of June 30, 2026, funds in the Morningstar strategic beta category skew slightly smaller and growthier than the Russell 3000 Index while showing very similar profitability.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The aggregate factor dollar is barely tilted, so buying small and value today is not obviously buying into a crowded trade.
insights.quote: Compared to the Russell 3000 Index, these funds skew slightly smaller and growthier, but with very similar profitability.

insights.claim: The average dollar in factor-based products is tilted toward growth rather than value, which cuts against the intuition that factor investing is predominantly a value trade.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: If factor money is net growthy, the value premium faces less flow-driven compression than the crowding narrative assumes.
insights.locator: And that style is more market-like than some might expect

insights.claim: Profitability, defined as operating income before depreciation and amortization minus interest expense scaled by book equity, is the characteristic on which strategic beta funds most closely match the broad market.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The profitability premium shows the least evidence of crowding, making quality-style tilts the least contested of the common factors on this evidence.

insights.claim: Aggregating the holdings characteristics of an entire fund category to describe the style of the average dollar invested is the diagnostic used to test whether factor strategies are competing away their own premiums.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: A repeatable, cheap crowding check: track category-level size, relative price, and profitability tilts versus a broad benchmark over time.
insights.quote: Aggregating their characteristics tells us the style of the average dollar invested in the group.

insights.claim: On the strategic beta sample there is little evidence that factor investors are attenuating the premiums associated with higher expected return stocks, though the conclusion is explicitly hedged to that one sample.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Supports staying invested in systematic size, value, and profitability tilts, while flagging that the test excludes non-strategic-beta factor capital such as active and hedge fund money.
insights.quote: Based on this sample, at least, there’s not much evidence factor investors are attenuating premiums associated with higher expected return stocks.
